title: .gitignore and good commits
summary: .gitignore keeps build output and secrets out of history; small, well-described commits make that history useful.

steps.title: .gitignore
body: Some files must never be committed: build output, editor settings, logs, and above all **secrets**. List them in a `.gitignore` file at the repo root (and commit *that* file):
# but keep this one example file
| `*.log` | any file ending `.log`, in any folder |
| `bin/` | any **folder** named `bin`, and everything in it |
| `!pattern` | un-ignore something an earlier line ignored |
Ignored files do not appear as `??` in `git status`, and `git add .` skips them.

steps.prompt: For a .NET web app: commit it, or ignore it?
steps.explain: Commit everything needed to build and run the project (sources, project files, lock files, config without secrets). Ignore anything generated, machine-specific, or secret.

steps.prompt: `.gitignore` contains `*.log` and `bin/`. None of these files are tracked yet. What does `git status -s` print? (Sorted by name.)
steps.explain: `*.log` matches `build.log` and `logs/today.log` in any folder; `bin/` hides the whole folder. The `.gitignore` file itself is untracked until you add it, and you should add it.

steps.prompt: `appsettings.Local.json` was committed last month. Today you add it to `.gitignore`, but `git status` still shows it as modified. Why, and what fixes it?
options: `.gitignore` only affects untracked files. Run `git rm --cached appsettings.Local.json` and commit, so Git stops tracking it but leaves it on disk
`.gitignore` needs `git add .gitignore` before it takes effect for any file
Ignore rules apply only after `git gc`
Run `git rm appsettings.Local.json`, which removes it from tracking and keeps the file
steps.explain: Once tracked, a file stays tracked. `git rm --cached` removes it from the index only; plain `git rm` deletes it from disk too. If it ever held a secret, the secret is still in old commits: rotate it (module 6).

steps.title: Commits worth reading
body: History is read far more often than it is written: by reviewers, by `git blame`, by you at 2 a.m. during an incident.
**One logical change per commit.** A bug fix, a rename and a reformat are three commits. Then each can be reviewed, reverted or cherry-picked alone.
Fix rounding in invoice totals                  <- subject: imperative, <= 50 chars, no period
Totals were summed as double and rounded once   <- blank line, then the body,
at the end, so some invoices were off by a      <- wrapped at 72. Explain WHY;
cent. Sum as decimal and round per line.           the diff already shows what.
Write the subject as a command: *"Fix rounding"*, not *"Fixed rounding"*. Test it: *"If applied, this commit will fix rounding."*

options: `Changes to OrderValidator.cs, also some cleanup and formatting.`
steps.explain: It is imperative, says what changes in behaviour, and fits in 50 characters. The others are vague, name files instead of intent, or mix several changes.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into a well-formed commit message.
lines: The provider returns 503 during deploys. We dropped
those events, so orders stayed unpaid. Retry three
times with backoff before giving up.
steps.explain: Subject, blank line, the body explaining why, blank line, then trailers such as issue references.
also: The provider returns 503 during deploys. We dropped
those events, so orders stayed unpaid. Retry three
times with backoff before giving up.

steps.prompt: Match each habit to the problem it prevents.
pairs: a revert that also undoes an unrelated fix
debug prints and stray files in the commit

steps.title: A commit message linter

build.unlocks: gitkit lint-msg now refuses sloppy commit messages.
build.title: Commit message linter
transform: // Your passing code from the code-dojo Git track.

prompt: Teams often enforce message rules in a `commit-msg` hook. Write `Lint(string message)` returning a list of problems, **in this order**, each at most once:
1. `"empty subject"`: the first line is empty or whitespace.
2. `"subject longer than 50"`: the first line has more than 50 characters.
4. `"no blank line after subject"`: there is a second line and it is not empty.
5. `"body line longer than 72"`: any line after the first is longer than 72.
Lines are separated by `\n`. A valid message returns an empty list.
solution: if (subject.EndsWith(".")) problems.Add("subject ends with a period");
if (lines.Length > 1 && lines[1] != "") problems.Add("no blank line after subject");
if (lines.Skip(1).Any(l => l.Length > 72)) problems.Add("body line longer than 72");
hints: `var lines = message.Split('\n');` then `lines[0]` is the subject.
Check each rule with its own `if`, in the given order.
template: Dojo.Eq("good message has no problems", new List<string>(), Lint("Fix rounding in invoice totals\n\nSum as decimal."));
Dojo.Eq("subject only is fine", new List<string>(), Lint("Add retry to webhook"));
Dojo.Eq("period", new List<string> { "subject ends with a period" }, Lint("Fix bug."));
Dojo.Eq("long subject", new List<string> { "subject longer than 50" }, Lint(new string('a', 51)));
Dojo.Eq("missing blank line", new List<string> { "no blank line after subject" }, Lint("Fix it\nbecause"));
Dojo.Eq("long body line", new List<string> { "body line longer than 72" }, Lint("Fix it\n\n" + new string('b', 73)));
Dojo.Eq("several problems in order", new List<string> { "subject longer than 50", "subject ends with a period", "no blank line after subject" },
